title: Repairing a 1960s Three-Handle Shower Valve: Seats, Stems, Diverter, and Trim
summary: This This Old House segment guides a homeowner through diagnosing and repairing a three-handle shower valve from a 1960s-era bathroom. The host explains the three-valve anatomy (hot and cold stems, a diverter, and a valve body behind the wall), demonstrates disassembly (removing escutcheons, extracting stems with tub sockets, and inspecting the diverter), and compares original parts to a modern replacement kit. The video emphasizes sourcing the correct parts, the importance of bonnet packing and gaskets to prevent leaks into the wall, and careful reassembly with properly aligned trim and labeled hot/cold handles. It also notes that three-valve configurations are less common today and discusses upgrading to a modern, pressure-balanced valve for safety. The closing tips cover locating parts via manufacturer markings, using a parts kit, and the value of a trim plate when upgrading the wall installation.
topics: Trim and escutcheon alignment against tile

sections.title: Valve anatomy and initial diagnosis
concepts: 1960s three-valve shower setup
Hot and cold supply lines and valve body behind wall
Diverter directing water to tub spout or shower head
sections.description: Introduction to the original three-valve shower in a 1960s bathroom and the basic function of hot/cold stems feeding a valve behind the wall, with a diverter that routes water to either the tub spout or the shower head. The host outlines the need to verify parts match and to understand why leaks may occur (into the wall or crawl space) when the system is not functioning correctly.

sections.title: Disassembly: removing escutcheons and stems
concepts: Turning off the main water supply
Protective drop cloth and drain protection
Escutcheon removal and identification
Using tub sockets to extract stems
sections.description: The homeowner protects the tub area, verifies the shutoff is off, and begins disassembly. The host identifies escutcheons, notes mismatched fasteners, demonstrates the correct method for removing escutcheons (clockwise to loosen, counterclockwise to remove), and uses specialized tub sockets to extract the valve stems because the valve body sits behind tile. The importance of matching parts to the original stem unit becomes evident as loosened parts reveal wear behind the wall.

sections.title: Stem, diverter, and seat inspection
concepts: Stem unit function and threads
Seat and bonnet relationship
Bonnet packing and gasket considerations
Comparison of old vs. new parts
sections.description: With the stems removed, the host exposes the cold stem and explains how the stem lifts and seals against the seat, and how the bonnet and bonnet gasket control leakage. The diverter’s role is described, and a side-by-side comparison shows that old and new parts can differ in thread length, washer size, and spline pattern, affecting compatibility and performance.

sections.title: Part compatibility and sourcing
concepts: Variability of stem units and splines
Why brand mismatches matter
Source options: manufacturer parts vs. repair parts kit
Specialty plumbing wholesalers
sections.description: The host emphasizes the diversity of stem units, noting that different brands use different spline counts and thread dimensions, so mixing handles is not reliable. He demonstrates that while matching original parts is ideal, a repair parts kit from a specialty wholesaler can provide all necessary components (handles, escutcheons, stems, diverter, seats, wrench) and a cap thread gasket for a proper wall seal.

sections.title: Replacement and reassembly: seats, stems, and trim
concepts: Installing new seats with a square insert
Using tub sockets to thread in stems and diverter
Tightening, but not over-tightening, to seat the components
Adjusting escutcheons and trimming to tile
sections.description: Replacement begins with seats, using a dedicated wrench to seat them. New stems and the diverter are installed and threaded in with tub sockets. The host stresses proper torque to avoid leaks and demonstrates how to tighten bonnet packing for a watertight seal. Trim adapters and escutcheons are threaded to align with the tile, and the escutcheon depth is adjusted to sit flush against the tile.

sections.title: Final assembly and labeling
concepts: Labeling hot and cold handles
Ensuring symmetry and consistency with original look
Using a parts kit that includes tools and gaskets
Cap thread gasket importance
sections.description: Handles are installed and labeled hot and cold. The host checks alignment and confirms the fixture resembles its original appearance, then shows that the kit includes all parts needed, including a cap thread gasket to seal the back of the wall. The importance of using the right tools and ensuring tight but not over-tight connections is reinforced.

sections.title: Code considerations and upgrade notes
concepts: Three-valve systems vs. modern pressure-balanced valves
Code requirements for anti-scald safety
When upgrading: wall plate and trim considerations
sections.description: The host notes that three-valve designs are not favored today due to safety concerns, particularly with pressure balance and scalding risk when other fixtures impact pressure. Upgrading to a modern, pressure-balanced valve is discussed as an option for new installations. The video also covers potential tile wall remodeling to install a single mixing valve with an opening plate for a cleaner upgrade when appropriate.
